Operator:
Good day, and welcome to the MedTech Innovations Q3 2023 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your telephone. Please note, this call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call will contain forward-looking statements, including expectations regarding our future performance, business outlook, and financial results. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Joining me on today's call are Alex Rivera, CEO; Michael Chen, CFO; Dr. Lisa Patel, Chief Technology Officer; and Tom Hargrove, Chief Commercial Officer.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. MedTech Innovations achieved record results this Q3, reflecting the strength of our diversified portfolio and our commitment to innovation.

Today, I will cover eight key aspects of our performance:
1. Procedure volume trends and market recovery commentary
2. FDA approvals and CE marks obtained
3. Impact of pricing and cost management initiatives
4. Capital equipment vs consumables mix trends
5. Revenue and margin guidance for the next quarter/year
6. R&D investment and innovation pipeline progress
7. Gross margin trends and supply chain commentary
8. SG&A expense management and efficiency gains

Michael will then provide a more detailed review of our financials. Dr. Patel will update us on our technology advancements, and Tom will discuss our market strategies. We'll then conclude with a Q&A session.

Now, let's get started with procedure volume trends and market recovery commentary. Michael, please provide some color there.

Michael Chen:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our Q3 procedure volume trends and provide some color on the broader market recovery dynamics, which were key drivers behind our 14% organic revenue growth this quarter. As you know, the medical devices sector has been navigating a multi-year recovery from the COVID-19 disruptions, with elective and semi-elective procedures resuming at varying paces across modalities and regions. I'm pleased to report that procedure volumes across our portfolio grew 16% year-over-year globally, accelerating from the 12% we saw in Q2, and marking our strongest quarterly performance since pre-pandemic levels.

Let me start with the headline numbers by therapeutic area, as this mix shift continues to underpin our outperformance versus peers. In structural heart, which now represents 42% of our MedTech segment revenue—up from 38% a year ago—global procedure volumes surged 24% YoY. TAVR, or transcatheter aortic valve replacement, was the standout, with volumes up 28%, driven by our next-gen EvoQ valve platform, which captured an incremental 220 basis points of US market share to 32%. This reflects the ongoing expansion into lower-risk and younger patient cohorts following the 2020 FDA approval expansions, similar to what we've seen at Edwards Lifesciences with their Sapien 3 Ultra. Our lower-profile delivery system and improved paravalvular leak rates have resonated with high-volume centers, where OR utilization has rebounded to 92% of 2019 levels per our Symphony Health claims data.

TMVR, or transcatheter mitral valve replacement, saw even stronger momentum at 35% volume growth, fueled by the full US launch of our TriAd clip system, which posted a 45% attach rate on TAVR cases in the quarter. This compares favorably to Abbott's MitraClip, where we've been gaining share through our differentiated leaflet-grasping technology and a 15% reduction in procedure time versus legacy systems. Pacemaker and ICD volumes in our CRM franchise grew 18% globally, with leadless pacing—led by our Aviator device—up 42%, as hospitals prioritize shorter stays and reduced infection risks amid ongoing nursing shortages.

Orthopedics, at 28% of our portfolio, delivered 13% volume growth, with robotic-assisted knee and hip procedures jumping 22% thanks to the integration of our OrthoNav 5.0 platform, which boasts a 98% accuracy rate in implant positioning. This positions us well against Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci in hybrid ORs, where we've seen a 10% uptick in bundled procedure adoption. Endoscopy volumes were more muted at 9% growth, reflecting softer GI screening amid persistent reimbursement pressures from CMS's 2024 APC cuts, but our single-use duodenoscope portfolio mitigated cannibalization risks and drove a 5% ASP uplift.

Regionally, the recovery story is bifurcated but broadly positive. In the US, which accounted for 52% of our Q3 volumes, procedures grew 19% YoY, outpacing the 15% industry average tracked by Definitive Healthcare. This acceleration was broad-based, with TAVR cases up 32% in the Northeast and Midwest heart centers, where staffing ratios have stabilized post the Great Resignation wave. We're also seeing tailwinds from the Biden administration's $1.2 trillion infrastructure bill indirectly boosting hospital capex for hybrid ORs—our installed base of structural heart cath labs grew 11% QoQ.

EMEA volumes rose 12% YoY, tempered by softer German DRG reimbursement for orthopedics—down 3% nominally—and lingering inflationary pressures on consumables. However, our UK and French TAVR franchises grew 20%, benefiting from NICE guidelines expanding indications to symptomatic patients under 75, akin to Medtronic's Evolut FX momentum. In APAC, we hit 22% growth, led by China at 31% with over 15,000 TAVR procedures logged via NHSA data—more than doubling YoY as local payers like the NRDL include our EvoQ at favorable pricing. Japan and India contributed via regulatory wins for our robotic ortho suite, where procedure mix shifted 8 points toward robotics amid an aging demographic—Japan's over-65 population now at 29%.

Diving deeper into market recovery dynamics, we're now at 98% of 2019 procedure volumes globally, up from 92% in Q2, per our normalized index adjusted for COVID deferrals. This compares to peers like Boston Scientific reporting 96% recovery in their WATCHMAN LAAO franchise and Stryker at 97% in orthopedics. Key enablers include resolved supply chain bottlenecks—our valve component yield rates hit 99.5%—and hospital procedure backlogs clearing at a 10-12% QoQ clip, per KLAS Research OR scheduling surveys. Headwinds persist, though: US labor costs up 7% YoY are capping elective scheduling, and China's zero-COVID echoes delayed 5% of planned cases into Q4.

Strategically, we're leaning into three initiatives to sustain this momentum. First, our Precision Procedure Ecosystem, a digital suite integrating AI-driven case planning with our robotics—piloted in 150 US sites—boosted procedure efficiency by 18%, enabling 12% more cases per OR day. Early data shows a 25% reduction in readmissions for TAVR, which should support ASP premiums under value-based bundles like CMS's LVEF modifier. Second, we're accelerating M&A in neuromodulation, where procedure volumes grew just 8% industry-wide; our $450M acquisition of NeuroPulse last month adds a next-gen SCS platform targeting chronic pain, with Phase III data showing 40% pain reduction at 24 months—poised to challenge Nevro's Algovita.

Third, regionally tailored commercialization: In emerging markets like Brazil and Southeast Asia, we're bundling devices with training via our Global Procedure Academy, driving 30% volume uplift in partnered hospitals. And in the US/EU, our focus on site-of-care shift to ASCs—now 22% of TAVR volumes versus 15% in 2021—leverages lower costs and our ambulatory-optimized kits.

Looking forward, we expect Q4 volumes to grow 15-17% YoY, with structural heart at the high end, assuming stable reimbursement and no new COVID variants. Risks include potential US PBM scrutiny on device pricing and Eurozone recession softening ortho electives, but our 65% gross margins on high-growth franchises provide resilience. Our pipeline remains robust, with five INDs filing by year-end, including a bioresorbable stent for peripheral artery disease.

Alex Rivera:
Excellent overview, Michael. Thank you. Now, moving on to our FDA approvals and CE marks obtained, which were pivotal this quarter.

Good afternoon, everyone—though it's morning here. Before diving deeper into financials, I want to highlight a pivotal quarter for our regulatory pipeline—one that underscores our leadership in the Medical Devices space and positions us for accelerated revenue growth across our key franchises: structural heart, neuromodulation, and minimally invasive robotics.

Let me start with the headline wins. In Q3, we secured FDA Premarket Approval for our next-generation EvoFlow™ Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement system, building on the success of our first-gen EvoFlow platform, which has captured 12% U.S. market share in the structural heart market since its 2021 launch. This PMA was granted following the successful completion of our IDE pivotal trial, the EVOLVE-2 study, which enrolled 850 high- and intermediate-risk patients across 45 U.S. sites. Key data points: we demonstrated a 95% procedural success rate, a 2.1% 30-day all-cause mortality—better than the benchmarked 2.5% from the PARTNER 3 trial—and a record-low 0.8% paravalvular leak rate at one year, thanks to our proprietary tri-leaflet bovine pericardial design and AI-optimized docking system.

This approval unlocks a $2.8 billion addressable U.S. TAM in the TAVR segment alone, where procedure volumes grew 18% YoY per our claims data analysis, driven by expanded indications into low-risk patients post-2020 guidelines from ACC/AHA. We're forecasting $450 million in incremental U.S. revenue from EvoFlow™ in FY24, ramping to $1.2 billion by FY26, with gross margins expanding to 72% on scale—up from 68% today—due to our vertical integration in laser cutting and tissue processing at our Galway, Ireland facility.

Complementing this, we received FDA 510(k) clearance for three platform expansions: our NeuroPulse™ RF ablation catheter for atrial fibrillation, our FlexiGuide™ steerable sheath for peripheral vascular access, and a software upgrade to our RoboAssist™ robotic navigation system incorporating real-time AI segmentation for coronary interventions. These clearances represent a 25% acceleration in our 510(k) submission cadence—we filed 12 in the first nine months of 2023 versus eight in all of 2022—reflecting efficiencies from our $150 million R&D investment in digital twins and virtual clinical simulations, which cut our average time-to-clearance by 22% to 7 months.

Shifting to Europe, I'm pleased to report CE Mark certifications under the new MDR for both EvoFlow™ TAVR and our full neuromodulation portfolio, including the AuraStim™ rechargeable SCS system for chronic pain. MDR compliance has been a sector-wide bottleneck—only 60% of legacy CE marks were renewed by Q2 2023 per Notified Body data—but our proactive pivot in 2021, with a dedicated 50-person regulatory team and post-market clinical follow-up studies exceeding 10,000 patient-years, got us across the finish line ahead of peers like Boston Scientific, whose Wayfinder™ cath faced delays last quarter.

Regionally, this dual FDA/CE momentum is transformative. In the EU5, where TAVR penetration lags the U.S. at 45 procedures per million versus 120, EvoFlow™ positions us to gain 300 basis points of share from Edwards Lifesciences' Sapien franchise, targeting €350 million in Eurozone sales in 2024 amid a 15% CAGR in structural heart per IQVIA medtech tracker. In Asia-Pacific, our CE Mark facilitates faster JDM alignment with PMDA, where we've seen a 28% YoY uptick in robotic-assisted procedures post our partnership with Terumo. Emerging markets like Brazil and India, via ANVISA and CDSCO pathways, now represent a $500 million TAM opportunity as we leverage these predicates.

Strategically, these approvals align with three core initiatives. First, our Breakthrough Device Designation pipeline, now at seven programs including a bioresorbable scaffold with polymer innovations reducing recoil to <5%. We've achieved an 85% Breakthrough grant rate from FDA YTD, up from 70% industry average, fast-tracking PMAs by 6-12 months. Second, we're addressing reimbursement headwinds: EvoFlow™ qualifies for NTAP status, adding $1,200 per case under CMS IPPS, critical as U.S. hospital medtech spend shifts to value-based bundles. Third, supply chain resilience—post-COVID, we've derisked with dual-sourcing of nitinol from our Plymouth, MN and Singapore plants, ensuring 99.5% on-time delivery even amid Red Sea disruptions.

Looking ahead, our regulatory funnel remains robust: 18 submissions pending globally, including two PMAs and five MDR renewals, with a projected 90% approval yield based on historical mock audits. This de-risks our FY24 guidance of 14-16% organic revenue growth and 25-30% EPS expansion, outpacing the medtech consensus of 8-10%.

In summary, these FDA and CE milestones aren't just checkboxes—they're revenue engines fueling our 5-year ambition to double structural heart share to 25% and enter the $15 billion robotics market.

Alex Rivera:
Outstanding progress on regulatory, team. Next, the impact of pricing and cost management initiatives. Over to you, Michael.

Michael Chen:
Good morning again, everyone. Today, I'd like to dive deep into one of the key drivers behind our strong financial performance: the impact of our pricing and cost management initiatives. These efforts delivered a combined $285 million in incremental adjusted EBITDA this quarter, contributing to our 12% year-over-year core revenue growth and 250 basis points of gross margin expansion. Let me break this down in detail, with specifics on strategies, execution, and forward-looking insights tailored to our Medical Devices portfolio.

Starting with pricing initiatives, we've seen robust execution across our key franchises: Cardiovascular, Orthopedics, and Endoscopy. Our average selling price grew 4.2% year-over-year on a constant currency basis, outpacing our historical 2-3% average. This was driven by a multi-pronged approach.

Value-based pricing and premium product mix shift: In Cardiovascular, our next-generation drug-eluting stents—like the InnoStent Elite, which just received expanded FDA labeling for complex PCI cases—commanded a 7% ASP premium over legacy products. This mix shift alone added 150 basis points to overall pricing. Similarly, in Orthopedics, our robotic-assisted knee implant system, the PrecisionKnee platform, benefited from GPO contracts with Vizient and Premier, where we secured tier-1 positioning, driving 5% ASP uplift.

Regional dynamics: In the US, which represents 55% of our revenue, pricing power remains strong due to favorable reimbursement dynamics under Medicare's IPPS updates. We realized 5.8% ASP growth here, partially offsetting list price concessions in bundled payment models. Europe, at 25% of sales, faced headwinds from Germany's DRG revisions and France's price caps on high-volume devices like our endoscopy scopes, limiting growth to 2.1%. However, our proactive tender wins in the UK NHS for our AI-enhanced colonoscopes mitigated this to just a 50 bps drag. In emerging markets—China and LATAM, 15% combined—we leveraged local manufacturing approvals to introduce tiered pricing, achieving 6% ASP growth via partnerships like our JV with Mindray.

Contract optimization: We renewed 85% of our US GPO agreements with above-market escalators averaging 3.5%, while selectively walking away from 10% of low-margin renewals. This disciplined approach protected our book of business against aggressive tactics from competitors like Boston Scientific in Electrophysiology.

These pricing tailwinds directly boosted revenue by $210 million sequentially, representing 60% of our total core growth.

Now, turning to cost management initiatives, we've embedded structural savings that are proving resilient amid supply chain volatility and inflation. Our adjusted gross margin expanded to 68.2%, up 260 bps year-over-year and 110 bps quarter-over-quarter—the highest in five years. Key levers included supply chain and procurement efficiencies: Raw material costs, particularly titanium for implants and high-performance polymers for catheters, rose 8% industry-wide due to post-COVID demand. We countered this with a $120 million annualized savings program via our global sourcing hub in Singapore. Dual-sourcing critical components reduced single-supplier risk—e.g., from Nitinol vendors—and our long-term contracts locked in 5% below-market pricing for resorbable scaffolds. Inventory turns improved to 4.8x from 4.2x, freeing $75 million in working capital.

Manufacturing optimization: Lean Six Sigma initiatives across our 12 global plants yielded 15% productivity gains. In our Galway facility—our hub for structural heart devices—we deployed Industry 4.0 automation, including AI-driven defect detection, slashing scrap rates by 22% on TAVR valves. Reshoring select orthopedics assembly to our new US plant in Arizona avoided 12% tariff exposure from China and qualified us for IRA tax credits, adding 30 bps to margins.

Indirect cost discipline: We optimized R&D spend to 11.2% of revenue (down from 12.1%), prioritizing high-ROI projects like our neuromodulation pipeline while deferring non-core innovation. Headcount was right-sized by 4% through attrition and offshoring non-strategic functions to India, delivering $45 million in OpEx savings without impacting new product launches.

Regionally, these efforts were most pronounced in Asia-Pacific, where forex headwinds from a stronger USD shaved 2% off reported margins, but local cost reductions fully offset this.

Strategic insights for the MedTech sector: In a landscape dominated by giants like Medtronic and Stryker, our initiatives differentiate us through 'precision economics'—aligning pricing with clinical outcomes data from real-world evidence studies, which we've shared via our Outcomes Registry. This has de-risked reimbursement in value-based care models like CMS's Bundled Payments for Care Improvement. Looking ahead, we expect pricing to contribute 3-4% to 2025 growth, with cost savings scaling to $400 million annualized as our Green Hills ERP system rolls out enterprise-wide. However, we remain vigilant on biosimilar erosion in biologics-adjacent devices and potential US PBM scrutiny.

In summary, these initiatives not only fortified our P&L—driving 18% adjusted EPS growth—but position us for sustained 10-12% organic growth through the cycle.

Alex Rivera:
Thanks, Michael—strong execution there. Next, capital equipment versus consumables mix trends.

Michael Chen:
Good morning, everyone. As we dive into our segment performance, I'd like to spend some time on one of our key profitability levers: the capital equipment versus consumables revenue mix. For those new to our story, this mix is foundational to our razor-and-blade business model, akin to what you've seen at leaders like Intuitive Surgical with da Vinci or Stryker in orthopedics. Capital equipment—think our flagship V-Core robotic surgical systems, next-gen imaging cath labs, and endovascular delivery platforms—drives the installed base and upfront sales. Consumables, including single-use procedure kits, guidewires, balloon catheters, and bioabsorbable stents, generate high-margin, recurring annuity revenue as procedures ramp on that base.

Let me start with the numbers. In Q3, total revenue reached $1.28 billion, up 14% year-over-year on a reported basis and 16% at constant currency. Breaking it down by mix: Capital equipment represented 32% of total revenue, or $410 million, up 8% YoY. This was driven by a 12% increase in unit volume for our V-Core Xi systems, partially offset by a modest 3% ASP contraction due to competitive pricing pressures in the U.S. hospital capex cycle.

Consumables now comprise a robust 68% of the mix, delivering $870 million, up 17% YoY and accelerating from 15% growth in Q2. This reflects 11% organic growth from higher procedure volumes on our 28,000+ global installed base—up 9% YoY—and a 4% tailwind from pricing actions on premium kits like our HelixGuide steerable catheters.

Over the trailing 12 months, the consumables mix has expanded by 250 basis points to 67%, pushing our overall gross margins to 68.2%—a 210 bps improvement YoY. This shift is no accident; it's the result of our disciplined focus on installed base expansion and utilization.

Trend analysis and drivers: Looking at trends, capital equipment sales have been lumpy but constructive. Q3 marked the strongest quarter for capital placements since pre-COVID peaks, with 420 V-Core systems shipped globally—exceeding our guidance midpoint. Utilization rates on the installed base hit 85% in robotics and 78% in our cardio interventions segment, up from 72% and 68% a year ago, respectively. This is fueling consumables pull-through, where our attach rates remain best-in-class at 1.7x per capital unit annualized.

That said, we're not immune to macro headwinds. Hospital capex budgets remain constrained amid high interest rates and staffing shortages—echoing what peers like Medtronic reported in their medtech segment. Capital growth slowed sequentially from Q2's 11% due to a $15 million inventory destock in Europe from a key distributor.

On the consumables side, the acceleration is broad-based: Robotics 20% YoY growth to $320 million, driven by 15% procedure volume growth in complex gyn and urologic cases. Our single-use EndoWeld instruments saw 25% uptake, reducing cross-contamination risks and aligning with FDA and EU MDR single-use mandates. Cardiovascular $280 million, up 16%, with strong demand for our AccelStent bioresorbable platforms amid the shift from permanent metal stents. Orthopedics and Spine $170 million, up 14%, bolstered by our Triad Cementless implants paired with robotic navigation kits.

Regional commentary: U.S. (52% of revenue): Consumables mix at 70%, up 300 bps YoY, thanks to CMS reimbursement tailwinds under the 2024 IPPS final rule, which boosted payments for robotic-assisted procedures by 4-6%. Capital was flat sequentially as elective volumes normalized post-respiratory season. Europe (28%): Mix at 65%, with consumables up 19% on robust V-Core adoption in Germany's DRG system and France's Hôpital 2.0 investments. However, capital dipped 2% due to MDR recertification delays for legacy cath lab equipment. APAC (15%): Highest growth at 22% for consumables, led by China's National Reimbursement Drug List inclusion for our stents, driving 30% procedure growth. Installed base here expanded 15% to 4,200 units. Emerging Markets (5%): Consumables up 25%, fueled by LATAM partnerships like our distribution deal with a major Mexican hospital chain, though capital remains nascent at 40 units.

Technical initiatives and strategic insights: Strategically, we're doubling down on mix optimization. R&D investments—up 18% to $220 million this year—target next-gen consumables like our AI-enabled SmartFlow catheters, which integrate real-time procedural analytics to boost efficiency by 20%. We've launched a $100 million share buyback tied to free cash flow from consumables, underscoring our confidence in 70%+ mix by FY2025.

Initiatives include installed base monetization: Our VitalConnect digital platform now links 65% of systems, enabling predictive maintenance and upsell of premium kits—adding 2-3% to consumables growth. Sustainability push: Transitioning 40% of kits to recyclable materials by 2025, preempting EU Green Deal regs and differentiating vs. competitors like Boston Scientific. M&A pipeline: We're eyeing bolt-on acquisitions in single-use endoscopy to accelerate mix shift, similar to Smith & Nephew's acquisition of CartiHeal.

Risks? Supply chain volatility for semiconductors in robotics could pressure capital ASPs by 2-3% next year, and potential U.S. Medicare cuts loom. But with a $2.5 billion backlog and 92% customer retention, our trajectory is solid. We guide Q4 consumables growth at 16-18%, capital at 7-9%, maintaining full-year mix expansion.

Alex Rivera:
Appreciate the detail, Michael. Now, revenue and margin guidance for the next quarter and year—your area.

Michael Chen:
Good morning, everyone. Before we move further, I'd like to provide our forward-looking guidance for the fourth quarter ending December 31, 2023, and the full fiscal year 2024. As always, these projections incorporate our latest visibility into procedural volumes, supply chain dynamics, foreign exchange headwinds, and the robust momentum across our core franchises in cardiovascular interventions, neuromodulation, and structural heart devices.

Starting with Q4 2023: We expect total revenue of $1.05 billion to $1.07 billion, representing 12% to 14% reported growth year-over-year, or 13% to 15% organic growth excluding the 2-point FX headwind from a stronger USD against the euro and yen. This compares favorably to our Q3 results of $980 million, which delivered 11% organic growth driven by strong U.S. adoption of our next-gen TAVR platform, the InnoFlow Ultra, and accelerating international uptake of our neuromodulation portfolio, including the NeuroPulse RF generator for chronic pain management.

Breaking it down by segment: Cardiovascular Interventions (52% of revenue): Expected to grow 15% organically, fueled by market share gains in drug-eluting stents with our Xypher-Z3 platform, which now holds a 28% U.S. share per the latest Millennium Research data, up from 24% a year ago. We're also seeing procedural tailwinds from the aging Baby Boomer demographic, with U.S. PCI volumes up 8% industry-wide per DAR 360 tracking. Structural Heart & Endovascular (28% of revenue): 18% organic growth, led by $220 million in InnoFlow Ultra sales as we lap easier comps and expand into Japan following PMDA approval in August. This positions us to challenge Edwards Lifesciences' dominance in low-risk TAVR indications. Neuromodulation & Other (20% of revenue): 10% organic growth, with strength in spinal cord stimulators amid a competitive landscape with Abbott's Proclaim XR, but offset by softer elective orthopedic procedures due to lingering reimbursement scrutiny from CMS on bundled payments.

Regionally: U.S. (65% of revenue): 16% organic growth, supported by our direct sales force expansion to 2,800 reps and hospital capital placements for our robotic-assisted endovascular suite, EchoNav 2.0. EMEA (20%): 12% growth, benefiting from single-digit PCI volume recovery post-energy crisis and new tenders in the UK NHS for DES. APAC ex-China (10%): 14% growth, driven by India and Southeast Asia penetration. China (5%): Flat to low-single-digit growth due to ongoing anti-corruption probes mirroring those impacting Johnson & Johnson and Medtronic, though our local JV partnerships are mitigating volume declines to under 5%.

On margins: We guide to adjusted gross margin expansion of 150 basis points to 68.5% to 69.5%, reflecting manufacturing efficiencies from our new Greenville, SC facility ramp-up—now at 85% capacity—and favorable mix from high-margin disposables (85%+ gross margins). Adjusted operating margin of 24.5% to 25.5%, up 200 bps sequentially, as SG&A leverage improves to 38% of revenue from better-than-expected rep productivity. Free cash flow conversion remains strong at 95%+ of adjusted net income, supporting our $500 million share repurchase authorization.

Now, turning to full-year 2024 guidance: We are raising our outlook to total revenue of $4.25 billion to $4.35 billion, implying 11% to 14% reported growth and 12% to 15% organic growth over FY 2023's expected $3.85 billion. This embeds modest 1% FX tailwinds assuming current rates, and excludes any inorganic contributions—we remain disciplined on M&A but are monitoring tuck-ins like the rumored NeuroStim assets from Nevro.

Key drivers for FY '24: Procedural volume tailwinds: Aging demographics and pent-up demand should drive 5-7% industry growth per Evaluate MedTech forecasts, with our exposure to high-growth areas like TAVR (projected 15% CAGR through 2028) and neuromodulation (12% CAGR). Pipeline milestones: Q1 launch of our AI-enhanced intravascular ultrasound system, VisioAI, integrating real-time plaque characterization to compete with Philips' Volcano platform—early trials show 20% faster pullbacks and 15% pullback adoption uplift. Full-year contribution: $150 million. Also, CE Mark for our next-gen WATCHMAN FLX Pro LAA occluder in H1, targeting Boston Scientific's market leadership. Technical initiatives: R&D investment at 12% of revenue ($510 million), focused on bioresorbable scaffolds and closed-loop neuromod devices. Supply chain resilience via dual-sourcing nitinol from Japan and Mexico, reducing lead times by 25% YoY. Margin trajectory: Adjusted gross margin of 69% to 70%, with 250 bps expansion from scale, pricing discipline (mid-single-digit ASP growth in U.S. contracts), and lower freight costs post-Red Sea disruptions. Adjusted EBITDA margin of 26% to 27%, up from 24.5% in FY '23, as we realize $100 million in Project Horizon cost-outs, including automation in catheter assembly.

Strategic insights: We're prioritizing market share in the $15 billion structural heart market, where we're gaining 150 bps annually through clinical data superiority—our latest TAVR pivotal showed 2.5% lower paravalvular leak vs. competitors. Reimbursement remains a watch item, with IRA-mandated device price transparency potentially pressuring ASPs by 2-3%, but our value-based contracts with 40% of U.S. IDNs mitigate this. Geopolitically, we're de-risking China exposure to under 4% of revenue by FY '25 via APAC diversification.

Risks to guidance include slower-than-expected hospital capex cycles, FX volatility, or delays in FDA 510(k)s. Conversely, upside could come from accelerated WATCHMAN adoption or bolt-on acquisitions.

We remain confident in delivering another year of above-market growth and margin expansion, positioning MedTech Innovations for sustained 12-15% organic CAGR through the decade.

Alex Rivera:
Solid guidance, Michael. Let's turn to R&D investment and innovation pipeline progress.

Michael Chen:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. As we wrap up a strong quarter with revenue of $1.8 billion, up 12% year-over-year on a constant currency basis, I'd like to dive deeper into our R&D engine—the lifeblood of MedTech Innovations. In the Medical Devices sector, where innovation drives over 70% of long-term revenue growth according to recent Deloitte benchmarks, we're leaning in aggressively. Our fiscal Q3 R&D investment totaled $168 million, representing 9.3% of revenue—up from 8.7% a year ago and in line with top-tier peers like Intuitive Surgical and Boston Scientific, who average 9-11%. For the full year FY24, we now guide to $650-675 million in R&D spend, a 14% increase YoY, funded through our robust free cash flow of $1.2 billion TTM and disciplined capex allocation.

This investment isn't just spend—it's strategically deployed across our four core franchises: Cardiovascular (42% of R&D), Neuromodulation & Robotics (28%), Orthopedics & Spine (20%), and Diagnostics & Wearables (10%). We're prioritizing high-growth adjacencies amid industry tailwinds like the aging global population—projected to drive a $250 billion TAM expansion by 2030 per Grand View Research—and the shift to value-based care, where procedural efficiency and outcomes data are paramount.

Let me highlight key progress in our 28-project pipeline, valued at an estimated $15 billion in peak sales potential. We're advancing 12 programs in late-stage development (Pivotal trials or regulatory submission), with five on track for commercialization in the next 18-24 months.

Cardiovascular Pipeline – Leading with Next-Gen Interventions: Our flagship is the CoreFlow™ TAVR system, a next-generation transcatheter aortic valve replacement platform building on our 25% U.S. market share in structural heart. We've completed enrollment in our 800-patient IDE pivotal trial, showing 95% procedural success and a 30-day mortality rate of just 1.2%—best-in-class versus Medtronic's CoreValve Evolut at 2.1%. Data readout is Q1 CY24, with FDA PMA submission targeted mid-2024 and EU CE Mark under MDR by year-end 2023. Early economics look compelling: projected ASP of $32,000, gross margins north of 75%, and a $4 billion addressable market growing at 18% CAGR. Complementing this, our ElastiCoat™ DCB—drug-coated balloon for below-the-knee PAD—hit 85% primary patency at 12 months in our ORBIT II follow-on study, outperforming Medtronic's IN.PACT at 78%. We're ramping U.S. limited market release post-510(k) clearance in July, with APAC rollout via our NMPA partnership in China accelerating amid their 20% procedural growth.

Neuromodulation & Robotics – AI-Enabled Precision: In neuromodulation, the NeuroPulse™ DBS platform—our directional deep brain stimulation system akin to Abbott's Infinity but with integrated AI burst modulation—advanced to full enrollment in a 450-patient ESSENTIAL trial for Parkinson's and essential tremor. Interim data shows a 52% motor score improvement at six months, versus 42% for competitors, with our proprietary SenseRx™ sensing reducing battery recharge needs by 40%. PMA filing is on deck for H1 2024. Robotics remains a $25 billion opportunity by 2028. Our da Vinci-competitive HugoFlex™ single-port robotic system is crushing milestones: 200-case surgeon training completed, with first-in-human trials in EU starting Q4 2023 under CE Mark pathway. Early sim-lab data indicates 25% faster procedure times in gyn and urology, targeting Stryker's Mako adjacency.
